jobs.prompt:
perf(cpp): memory optimisation project for the native gateway, driven by the real Codex client against a programmed-reply model

CONTEXT (you have no other context than this prompt and the repository)
You start from branch `claude/cpp-gateway-port` of ubiquity/ai.ubq.fi: the native C++20 gateway (`cpp/gateway/`), C++ only (do NOT install or run Bun, Node, Deno, Rust or Cargo; the `codex` CLI is ALREADY installed on your runner and is the one exception you may run). Read `cpp/gateway/README.md`, `docs/ARCHITECTURE.md`, `docs/RUNTIME.md`, `docs/CI.md` (driver: `bash cpp/gateway/tools/ci-build.sh --config release <test>`), `bench/codex_memory/` and `bench/request_path/` (how the packaged gateway is launched against scripted mock upstreams), and `docs/findings/cppgw-memory-20261121.md` (a first investigation). Your branch becomes a pull request; your final message is its body (plain language, before/after table).

WHY THE FIRST INVESTIGATION WAS NOT ENOUGH: it used a scripted HTTP client and a SYNTHETIC 4.8 MB catalog of 535 models with eight API keys and 16 usage rows, found the catalog copies, and fixed them (benchmark: 94 -> 23 MiB). On the real deployment with the real Codex CLI the fixed build still goes from 3 MiB idle to about 50 MiB of anonymous memory after ONE Codex session, with a peak resident size of about 112 MiB, and the previous build grew to 145 MiB after about 15 requests. So the benchmark did not model what production does. Real shape of what production serves and stores (sizes only, measured on the deployment):
- `GET /v1/models?client_version=0.171.0` (the Codex catalog): 389 kB, 15 models; almost all bytes are `model_messages` (256 kB total, up to 69 kB per model, only 6 distinct values across models) and `base_instructions` (110 kB total, up to 28 kB). Plain `GET /v1/models`: 45 kB, 535 entries.
- KV store: 512,415 rows, 183 MiB of values in a 1 GB SQLite file. Rows and value bytes by key prefix: (`uos_ai`,`api_key_usage`) 413,480 rows / 109 MiB / max 0.4 kB; (`uos_ai`,`sentinel_replay`) 10,595 / 32 MiB / max 48 kB; (`uos_ai`,`paid_fallback`) 47,089 / 21 MiB; (`ubq_ai`,`api_keys`) 17,786 / 9.8 MiB; (`uos_ai`,`admin_error_log`) 6,948 / 3 MiB; (`uos_ai`,`provider_capacity`) 3,116 / 3 MiB; (`embeddings`,`v2`) 848 / 2.7 MiB; (`uos_ai`,`metered_quota`) 2,051; (`uos_ai`,`prompt_cache_analytics`) 6,792; (`uos_ai`,`prompt_cache_telemetry_gate`) 2,848; (`uos_ai`,`sentinel_incident`) 538; catalog chunks 10 rows / 0.5 MiB; `kernel_auth` 72; `provider_health` 52; one `codex_auth` pool row.
The prime suspects are therefore NOT the catalog but whatever an authenticated request touches in those large families: loading or indexing all API keys, scanning or aggregating `api_key_usage`, quota/usage/capacity caches without bounds, replay retention scans, JSON DOMs of rows kept alive, per-request state that is never released, and allocator retention after such transients.

YOUR MACHINE: GitHub-hosted Linux ARM64 runner, Ubuntu 26.04, 4 CPUs, 16 GB, sudo, network. `sudo apt-get install -y clang ninja-build pkg-config ccache libboost-json-dev libboost-container-dev libssl-dev libsqlite3-dev zlib1g-dev libicu-dev libbrotli-dev libzstd-dev` gives a toolchain that builds this tree (the CI workflow shows the exact package list and how it builds the pinned SQLite: do the same). The environment has `CCACHE_DIR` set to a directory that is restored before and saved after your job; `ccache` is installed.


RULES
- The runner holds a model gateway token used by YOUR OWN agent session: never print it, never write it to a file, and never point the gateway under test or the test `codex` at the real model gateway. The test Codex must use a throwaway CODEX_HOME, a dummy key, and talk ONLY to the local gateway under test, which talks ONLY to your local programmed-reply upstream. No real provider traffic.
- Your process can be restarted without warning and then knows only what is committed: commit after each step; keep a checklist and every measurement in `cpp/gateway/docs/findings/cppgw-memory-2-20261121.md`. No foreground command longer than about 10 minutes (run load in the background and poll).
- Do not delete or weaken tests. Behaviour (responses, status codes, stored data, accounting, quota decisions) must not change; security limits must not be loosened.

TASK
1. HARNESS (`cpp/gateway/bench/codex_real/`): (a) a fixture generator that populates a state database with the row families, counts and value sizes listed above (use the gateway's own writers/test helpers so encodings are real; make one API key the "active client" with a realistic share of usage rows, e.g. 5,000, and spread the rest over the other keys), a 15-model Codex catalog with the byte sizes above, and a Codex auth pool; (b) a programmed-reply upstream ("synthetic model") speaking the provider protocol the gateway's Codex/ChatGPT path expects, with scripted streamed replies: plain text of 50 tokens, long text of 4,000 tokens, a reply with reasoning items, and tool-call turns (`shell`/`apply_patch` style function calls) so the client sends follow-up requests with growing context; (c) a driver that runs the REAL `codex` CLI (`codex exec`, throwaway CODEX_HOME with a provider block pointing at the gateway under test, wire_api responses, model catalog URL pointing at the gateway) for N sessions: single-turn, multi-turn with 10 tool round-trips (context growing to several hundred kB), and resumed sessions; and (d) a sampler that records for the gateway process, after start and after every session: VmRSS, RssAnon, VmHWM, `[heap]` and anonymous mappings from smaps, `mallinfo2` numbers if exposed, plus requests served. Run 1, 10, 100 and 500 sessions of the mix.
2. LIVE TELEMETRY: add to the gateway's `/health` (and the terminal request log line) cheap memory fields: resident and anonymous bytes read from `/proc/self/statm`/`smaps_rollup`, allocator in-use and free bytes (`mallinfo2`), and the byte size and entry count of every in-process cache (name each cache). No per-request cost beyond reading counters; no secrets. This is how the operator will watch memory in production.
3. ATTRIBUTE with `heaptrack` (or massif / malloc hooks with backtraces): top sites by retained bytes after a session and by peak bytes during it, separately for: authentication of the API key, quota/usage accounting, catalog, request body handling, streaming relay, terminal logging/telemetry, replay recording. State for each whether it is one-time, per-request growth, bounded cache, unbounded cache, or allocator retention (measure what `malloc_trim(0)` gives back).
4. FIX, largest first, one commit each with before/after from the harness: no full-table loads or scans where a keyed read or a bounded range read answers the question; bounded caches with explicit limits in `include/uos/rt/limits.hpp` and eviction; streaming instead of materialising large values; release of per-request state; deliberate SQLite `cache_size`/`mmap_size`; allocator settings only where the evidence shows retention. Keep it simple and standard; no custom allocator.
5. GUARD: make the harness a CI-runnable check (short profile: start, 20 real Codex sessions) that fails if anonymous memory after the run, or peak resident memory, exceeds budgets you derive from the final numbers plus about 30%; wire it into `.github/workflows/cpp-gateway-ci.yml` as one job if `codex` is available on the hosted runner image without installing Node (if it is not, keep the scripted-client variant in CI and document how to run the real-client variant).
Verification: tests linking changed files in release and `--config asan`; one full release shard; `python3 cpp/gateway/tools/links.py --check`.

DONE WHEN
The report shows, for the real-client mix on the realistic state, where memory goes (with profiler evidence), the fixes with before/after, and a flat line from 100 to 500 sessions. Targets: under 25 MiB anonymous after the first session, under 40 MiB after 500, peak resident under 80 MiB; if a target cannot be met say exactly what holds the memory and why it is needed.
